newsitem.title: USA: McDonnell-Douglas CEO sees July merger decision.
newsitem.headline: McDonnell-Douglas CEO sees July merger decision.

text.p: The CEO of McDonnell-Douglas Corp predicted Wednesday that the Federal Trade Commission will act on his company's proposed merger with Boeing Co by mid-July, and attacked the European Union for seeking a "war" over the transaction.
"The FTC will rule before the middle of July," Harry Stonecipher told reporters.
That timing would mean that the United States had completed action on the proposed merger before the European Union ran up against its own deadline for judging the transaction at the end of July.
Stonecipher said the public statements of EU Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert were "totally inappropriate."
"It's obvious he wants a war but I don't want a war," he said.
Stonecipher charged that van Miert's "prejudicial" comments about the merger had driven down the value of McDonnell-Douglas stock.
"He's influencing the stockmarket," Stonecipher said. "So why is he doing that?"
Van Miert told Reuters last month, and has reiterated his view since, that the merger cannot be permitted to take place so long as Boeing has exclusive 20-year contracts with two commercial airlines.
"To hold the merger hostage for that is totally inappropriate," Stonecipher said.
Stonecipher said that one of the Boeing contracts was reached before the merger was announced and "Mr. Van Miert didn't say a word."

Stonecipher, when asked, denied that Boeing and McDonnell-Douglas had speeded up the delivery of millions of documents to the FTC in order to assure that the United States ruled on the merger before the EU.
Once all of the documents are delivered to the FTC -- and Stonecipher said they would be delivered by early June -- the U.S. goverment has only 20 business days to reach a decision.
But if the government finds that the merger is unacceptable unless it is modified, the clock would stop until a new, restructured agreement was reached.
The FTC could also decide to forbid the merger of the two companies as anticompetitive.
Final approval by the government would be through a vote of the five-member FTC.

Meanwhile, the EU is operating on a different time schedule. Van Miert said this week that it would complete its investigation within 10 days, and send a statement to Boeing and McDonnell-Douglas outlining any problems it has with the merger. The next step would be a closed hearing to consider the views of the companies.

Van Miert has said the final deadline for EU action would be at the end of July. If the EU found the transaction to be anticompetitive, it could levy a fine of up to 10 percent of the combined companies' annual worldwide revenue.

The Europeans are considering only the effect on competition within commercial aviation. Europe is home to Airbus Industrie, which would be the only competitor to Boeing for large commercial aircraft after the merger.
But the Americans are considering the effect on both the commercial airline industry and on military supplies, which account for a large part of Boeing's and McDonnell-Douglas's business.
